How can coin flips compute $\pi$? The answer is a quintessential example of the *Monte Carlo principle*:

::: {.callout-important title="The Monte Carlo principle"}
Write the quantity we want as the expectation of a random variable, then estimate that expectation by an average of many samples.
:::

This chapter works through three questions, with $\pi$ as the running example.

1. How do we write $\pi$ as an expectation? We give two ways: points in a circle, and needles on a floor.
2. How accurate is the resulting estimate, and how fast does it improve as we add samples?
3. Are randomness-based methods faster or slower than non-random methods?

Along the way, we review the basics of probability that we'll need throughout the course.

## The circle estimator

Inscribe the unit circle in the square $[-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]$. A point chosen uniformly from the square lands inside the circle with probability equal to the ratio of the two areas,
$$P(X^2 + Y^2 \leq 1) = \frac{\pi}{4}.$$
So $\pi$ is four times a probability, and a probability is the expectation of an indicator. Let $(X, Y)$ be uniformly distributed on the square and define
$$
I(X, Y) = \mathbf{1}_{\{X^2 + Y^2 \leq 1\}} = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } X^2 + Y^2 \leq 1 \text{ (inside the circle)}, \\
0 & \text{if } X^2 + Y^2 > 1 \text{ (outside the circle)}.
\end{cases}
$$
Then $I \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi/4)$ and $\pi = 4\,\mathbb{E}[I]$. Replacing the expectation by a sample average gives our first estimator.

::: {#def-circle-estimator}
## The circle estimator
Given $N$ independent uniform points $(X_1, Y_1), \ldots, (X_N, Y_N)$ in the square, write $I_i = I(X_i, Y_i)$ and estimate $\pi$ by
$$\hat{\pi}_N = \frac{4}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} I_i = \frac{4 \cdot (\text{number of points inside the circle})}{N}.$$
:::

By linearity of expectation, $\mathbb{E}[\hat\pi_N] = 4\,\mathbb{E}[I] = \pi$ for every $N$: the estimator is *unbiased*.

The app below draws $N$ uniformly random points in the square and computes $\hat\pi_N$.

### Quantifying uncertainty

One way to quantify uncertainty in an unbiased estimator is via the *standard error*, $$\text{SE}(\hat\pi_N) = \sqrt{\text{Var}(\hat\pi_N)}.$$

::: {#exr-pi-variance}
## Standard error
Let $I_1, \ldots, I_N$ be as in @def-circle-estimator.

a. Compute $\text{Var}(I)$.
b. Compute $\text{Var}(\hat{\pi}_N)$ and $\text{SE}(\hat{\pi}_N)$. Where do you use independence?
c. How does $\text{SE}(\hat{\pi}_N)$ change with $N$?
d. How many times more points does one more correct decimal place cost?
e. Find the smallest $N$ for which $\text{SE}(\hat{\pi}_N) \le 0.001$.
:::


::: {#exr-pi-decimal}
## Checking the rate
Compare the *Standard error* in [the app](#pi-app) at $N = 100$ and at $N = 10{,}000$. Does the ratio match your answer to @exr-pi-variance (c)?
:::

Part (c) is the central fact of Monte Carlo:

::: {.callout-important title="The $N^{-1/2}$ rate"}
The standard error of an average of $N$ i.i.d. samples with finite variance falls like $N^{-1/2}$, whatever the problem. Only the constant depends on the problem.
:::

You should find that each extra correct digit costs 100 times as many samples. @fig-pi-convergence repeats the experiment many times. The first chart shows that the estimates do converge to $\pi$, and the second confirms that the error falls like $N^{-1/2}$, as @exr-pi-variance predicts.


```{ojs}
//| output: false
// Log-spaced sample sizes up to 10,000, so the runs read evenly on a log axis.
piRunCounts = checkpoints(10000, 24)
piRuns = runningCircleEstimates(VM.sampling.seededRandom(42), piRunCounts, 8)
piErrors = randomCircleErrors(VM.sampling.seededRandom(43), checkpoints(10000), 200)
```



```{ojs}
//| output: false
// The analysis figures (convergence and error plots) are static Observable
// Plot charts with a key under them, the way Visual Math Lab draws its
// convergence plots: nothing to zoom, so no modebar and no fullscreen.
// These functions read chartColors, so every figure built with them
// redraws on a dark-mode toggle.

// A chart with a Plot.legend key under it, and an optional title above.
// `key` is [{label, color}], in order. The title is a plain div rather than
// Plot's own `title` option, which renders an <h2> and so takes the page's
// section-heading style.
function piFigure(chart, key, title) {
  const domain = [], range = []
  for (const row of key) {
    domain.push(row.label)
    range.push(row.color)
  }
  const figure = document.createElement("div")
  // Plot charts have a fixed width; center the chart and its key in the column.
  figure.style.cssText = "width: fit-content; max-width: 100%; margin-inline: auto"
  if (title) {
    const heading = document.createElement("div")
    heading.textContent = title
    heading.style.cssText = "font-weight: 600; text-align: center; color: var(--vm-text)"
    figure.append(heading)
  }
  figure.append(chart, Plot.legend({color: {domain, range}}))
  return figure
}

// "10⁻³" for 0.001: tick labels for a log axis whose ticks are powers of ten.
function piPowerOfTen(value) {
  const superscripts = {"-": "⁻", "0": "⁰", "1": "¹", "2": "²", "3": "³", "4": "⁴", "5": "⁵", "6": "⁶", "7": "⁷", "8": "⁸", "9": "⁹"}
  let exponent = ""
  for (const ch of String(Math.round(Math.log10(value)))) exponent += superscripts[ch]
  return `10${exponent}`
}

// Every power of ten from `lo` to `hi`.
function piDecades(lo, hi) {
  const ticks = []
  for (let k = Math.ceil(Math.log10(lo) - 1e-9); k <= Math.floor(Math.log10(hi) + 1e-9); k++) ticks.push(10 ** k)
  return ticks
}

// A log axis over [lo / pad, hi * pad] with a tick at each power of ten
// inside it, and none outside, where Plot would draw them past the frame.
// Only decades are ticked, so the x axis reads like the y axis instead of
// carrying every minor tick.
function piLogAxis(lo, hi, options, pad = 1) {
  const domain = [lo / pad, hi * pad]
  return {type: "log", domain, ticks: piDecades(domain[0], domain[1]), tickFormat: piPowerOfTen, ...options}
}

// The width of one panel of a two-column figure: half the page column, less
// the gap between the columns. Quarto stacks layout-ncol panels below 768px,
// and each panel then gets the whole column. OJS's `width` follows the
// column, so the charts redraw to fill it when the window resizes.
piPanelWidth = {
  if (window.innerWidth < 768) return width
  return Math.floor((width - 24) / 2)
}

// Running estimates: one line per run against N ≥ `from`, and a dashed line
// at π. Without a `yDomain`, the y axis fits every plotted estimate, so no
// run leaves the frame.
function piRunsFigure({counts, runs, title, xLabel, yDomain, from = 0, chartWidth = piPanelWidth}) {
  const rows = []
  let lo = Math.PI, hi = Math.PI
  for (let r = 0; r < runs.length; r++) {
    for (let i = 0; i < counts.length; i++) {
      if (counts[i] < from || runs[r][i] === null) continue
      rows.push({run: r, n: counts[i], estimate: runs[r][i]})
      lo = Math.min(lo, runs[r][i])
      hi = Math.max(hi, runs[r][i])
    }
  }
  let domain = yDomain
  if (!domain) {
    const range = VM.plotting.paddedRange([lo, hi], {relativePadding: 0.05, minPadding: 0})
    domain = [range.lo, range.hi]
  }
  const runColor = VM.plotting.alpha(chartColors.fn, 0.6)
  const chart = Plot.plot(VM.plotting.plotOptions({
    width: chartWidth, height: 300, marginLeft: 46, marginBottom: 40,
    x: piLogAxis(Math.max(from, counts[0]), counts[counts.length - 1], {label: xLabel, labelAnchor: "center", tickFormat: "~s"}),
    y: {domain, label: "π estimate"},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(rows, {x: "n", y: "estimate", z: "run", stroke: runColor, strokeWidth: 1.5, clip: true}),
      Plot.ruleY([Math.PI], {stroke: chartColors.alt, strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "6,4"})
    ]
  }))
  return piFigure(chart, [{label: "Independent runs", color: runColor}, {label: "π", color: chartColors.alt}], title)
}

// Error decay: the RMS error over many runs, the band holding the middle 80%
// of runs, and a slope −1/2 reference raised above the band to compare with,
// over N ≥ `from`. Without a `yDomain`, the y axis fits the plotted values;
// with one, it stays put and anything outside is clipped.
function piErrorFigure({errors, title, xLabel, yDomain, from = 0, chartWidth = piPanelWidth}) {
  const last = errors[errors.length - 1]
  const rows = []
  for (const p of errors) {
    if (p.n >= from) rows.push({...p, reference: 2.5 * last.error * Math.sqrt(last.n / p.n)})
  }
  let lo = Infinity, hi = 0
  for (const row of rows) {
    lo = Math.min(lo, row.lo)
    hi = Math.max(hi, row.hi, row.reference)
  }
  const bandColor = VM.plotting.alpha(chartColors.fn, 0.15)
  const chart = Plot.plot(VM.plotting.plotOptions({
    width: chartWidth, height: 300, marginLeft: 46, marginBottom: 40,
    x: piLogAxis(Math.max(from, errors[0].n), last.n, {label: xLabel, labelAnchor: "center", tickFormat: "~s"}),
    y: yDomain ? piLogAxis(yDomain[0], yDomain[1], {label: "|estimate − π|"}) : piLogAxis(lo, hi, {label: "|estimate − π|"}, 1.25),
    marks: [
      Plot.areaY(rows, {x: "n", y1: "lo", y2: "hi", fill: bandColor, clip: true}),
      Plot.line(rows, {x: "n", y: "reference", stroke: chartColors.ink, strokeWidth: 1.5, strokeDasharray: "6,4", clip: true}),
      Plot.line(rows, {x: "n", y: "error", stroke: chartColors.fn, strokeWidth: 2, clip: true}),
      Plot.dot(rows, {x: "n", y: "error", fill: chartColors.fn, r: 2, clip: true})
    ]
  }))
  return piFigure(chart, [
    {label: "RMS error", color: chartColors.fn},
    {label: "Middle 80% of runs", color: bandColor},
    {label: "Slope −1/2", color: chartColors.ink}
  ], title)
}
```

::::

Confidence intervals put a probability on the size of the error. By the central limit theorem, for large $N$ the estimate $\hat\pi_N$ is approximately normal, with mean $\pi$ and standard deviation $\text{SE}(\hat\pi_N)$.

::: {#exr-pi-clt}
## Confidence intervals
a. Write an approximate 95% confidence interval for $\pi$ centered at $\hat{\pi}_N$, for large $N$. The standard error depends on $\pi$ itself, which we don't know: what can you use in its place?
b. Use your formula from @exr-pi-variance to compute the half-width $1.96\,\text{SE}(\hat\pi_N)$ of this interval at $N = 1000$.
c. Set [the app](#pi-app) to $N = 1000$ and click *Draw new points* 20 times. Each time, record whether $|\text{estimate} - \pi|$ is below your half-width from (b). How many misses do you expect? How many did you get?
:::

## Buffon's needle

A second method to estimate $\pi$ by random sampling goes back to Buffon in 1777. Take a floor made of parallel strips of wood, each of width $t$, and drop a needle of length $\ell \le t$ onto it at random. What is the probability that the needle lies across a line between two strips? The answer involves $\pi$, so counting the needles that cross gives us a way to estimate $\pi$.


The app below drops $N$ needles of length $\ell$ on lines spaced $t = 1$ apart and colors the ones that cross a line. Leave the *Shape* switch on *Needle* for now; the noodle is the subject of @rem-noodle.


```{ojs}
//| output: false
buffonMaxN = 10000
buffonDefaultSeed = 1
buffonDefaultN = 100
buffonDefaultLength = 0.8
buffonShapeOptions = ["Needle", "Noodle"]
// Lines y = 0, 1, ..., 6 (spacing t = 1) across a board 8 wide.
buffonSpacing = 1
buffonWidth = 8
buffonHeight = 6

buffonTraceOptions = ["Crossing a line", "Not crossing", "Lines"]
buffonTraceColors = new Map([
  ["Crossing a line", chartColors.alt],
  ["Not crossing", chartColors.fn],
  ["Lines", chartColors.muted]
])
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// buffonParseLength: the length a field's text names, or null when it isn't
// one -- empty, mid-typing, not positive, or longer than the line spacing,
// where the formula 2ℓ/(πt) stops holding.
function buffonParseLength(text) {
  const parsed = VM.expressions.makeNumber(window.math, text)
  if (parsed === null || !Number.isFinite(parsed) || parsed <= 0 || parsed > buffonSpacing) return null
  return parsed
}
```



```{ojs}
//| output: false
// buffonLength: the typed length, or the default while the field is invalid.
buffonLength = {
  const parsed = buffonParseLength(buffonLengthInput)
  if (parsed === null) return buffonDefaultLength
  return parsed
}
```

{
  // Drops as one trace per color, polylines separated by nulls -- a
  // single trace draws thousands of segments far faster than one trace each.
  const crossX = [], crossY = [], otherX = [], otherY = []
  for (let i = 0; i < buffonN; i++) {
    let xs = otherX, ys = otherY
    if (buffonNeedles.crossings[i] > 0) {
      xs = crossX
      ys = crossY
    }
    xs.push(...buffonNeedles.xs[i], null)
    ys.push(...buffonNeedles.ys[i], null)
  }

  const lineX = [], lineY = []
  for (let k = 0; k * buffonSpacing <= buffonHeight; k++) {
    lineX.push(-0.5, buffonWidth + 0.5, null)
    lineY.push(k * buffonSpacing, k * buffonSpacing, null)
  }

  const data = []
  if (buffonShow.has("Lines")) {
    data.push({x: lineX, y: lineY, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: "Lines", showlegend: false,
      line: {color: chartColors.muted, width: 1.5}, hoverinfo: "skip"})
  }
  if (buffonShow.has("Not crossing")) {
    data.push({x: otherX, y: otherY, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: "Not crossing", showlegend: false,
      line: {color: chartColors.fn, width: 2}, hoverinfo: "skip"})
  }
  if (buffonShow.has("Crossing a line")) {
    data.push({x: crossX, y: crossY, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: "Crossing a line", showlegend: false,
      line: {color: chartColors.alt, width: 2}, hoverinfo: "skip"})
  }

  return buffonPlot(data, {
    xaxis: {range: [-0.5, buffonWidth + 0.5], zeroline: false, showgrid: false, showticklabels: false, ticks: "", constrain: "domain"},
    yaxis: {range: [-0.6, buffonHeight + 0.6], zeroline: false, showgrid: false, showticklabels: false, ticks: "", scaleanchor: "x", constrain: "domain"},
    hovermode: false,
    uirevision: "static",
    autosize: true
  })
}

### Estimating the probability

Up to sliding along the lines, a drop is determined by two numbers:

- the angle $\theta \in [0, \pi)$ the needle makes with the lines, and
- the distance $d \in [0, t/2]$ from its center to the *nearest* line.


::: {#exr-buffon-uniform}
## The model
a. There is no uniform distribution on the plane. What should dropping the needle "at random" mean, and why is that enough?
b. Under your answer to (a), why is $(\theta, d)$ uniformly distributed on the rectangle $[0, \pi) \times [0, t/2]$ (the *All needle drops* panel of @fig-buffon-setup)?
:::

{
  const theta = buffonFigDrop.theta
  const d = buffonFigDrop.d
  const half = buffonFigLength / 2
  const h = half * Math.sin(theta)
  const tipX = -half * Math.cos(theta)
  const tipY = d - h
  const upperX = -tipX
  const upperY = d + h
  // Which way the lower tip leans: 1 for left, -1 for right. Labels go on the
  // side that keeps them clear of the needle.
  let side = 1
  if (tipX > 0) side = -1

  // The arc marking the angle between the needle and the level of its center.
  const arcX = [], arcY = []
  for (let k = 0; k <= 30; k++) {
    const angle = Math.PI + theta * k / 30
    arcX.push(0.11 * Math.cos(angle))
    arcY.push(d + 0.11 * Math.sin(angle))
  }

  const segment = (x, y, color, width, dash) => ({
    x, y, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", showlegend: false, hoverinfo: "skip",
    line: {color, width, dash}
  })
  const data = [
    // Where the center can be: every point within t/2 of the bold line.
    {x: [-0.95, 0.95, 0.95, -0.95, -0.95], y: [-0.5, -0.5, 0.5, 0.5, -0.5], type: "scatter", mode: "lines", fill: "toself",
      fillcolor: VM.plotting.alpha(chartColors.muted, 0.12), showlegend: false, hoverinfo: "skip", line: {width: 0}},
    // Three lines, with the one nearest the center in bold.
    segment([-0.95, 0.95], [-1, -1], chartColors.muted, 1.5, "solid"),
    segment([-0.95, 0.95], [1, 1], chartColors.muted, 1.5, "solid"),
    segment([-0.95, 0.95], [0, 0], chartColors.ink, 2.5, "solid"),
    segment([0.8, 0.8], [0, 1], chartColors.muted, 1, "dot"),
    segment([Math.min(tipX, -0.2), Math.max(tipX, 0.2)], [d, d], chartColors.ink, 1, "dot"),
    segment([tipX, tipX], [tipY, d], chartColors.warn, 2.5, "dash"),
    segment([0, 0], [0, d], chartColors.alt, 2.5, "solid"),
    segment(arcX, arcY, chartColors.ink, 1.5, "solid"),
    segment([tipX, upperX], [tipY, upperY], chartColors.fn, 5, "solid"),
    {x: [0], y: [d], type: "scatter", mode: "markers", showlegend: false, hoverinfo: "skip",
      marker: {color: chartColors.fn, size: 10}}
  ]

  const label = (x, y, text, color) => ({x, y, text, showarrow: false, font: {color, size: 15}})
  const thetaLabelAngle = Math.PI + theta / 2
  return buffonFigNeedlePlot(data, {
    title: {text: "One needle drop"}, margin: {t: 40, l: 10, r: 10, b: 10},
    xaxis: {range: [-1, 1], visible: false, fixedrange: true, constrain: "domain"},
    yaxis: {range: [-1.05, 1.05], visible: false, fixedrange: true, scaleanchor: "x", constrain: "domain"},
    annotations: [
      label(side * 0.05, d / 2, "d", chartColors.alt),
      label(tipX - side * 0.05, (tipY + d) / 2, "h", chartColors.warn),
      label(0.18 * Math.cos(thetaLabelAngle), d + 0.18 * Math.sin(thetaLabelAngle), "θ", chartColors.ink),
      label(upperX / 2 + side * 0.09 * Math.sin(theta), (d + upperY) / 2 - 0.09 * Math.abs(Math.cos(theta)), "ℓ/2", chartColors.fn),
      label(0.85, 0.5, "t", chartColors.muted)
    ],
    hovermode: false, uirevision: "static", autosize: true
  }, buffonFigConfig)
}

::: {#exr-buffon-region}
## The crossing probability
a. In the *One needle drop* panel, express $h$ in terms of $\ell$ and $\theta$. Does your formula still hold when $\theta > \pi/2$?
b. For which values of $d$ does the needle cross a line? Where do you use $\ell \le t$?
c. Sketch the region of the $(\theta, d)$ rectangle where the needle crosses a line, and use it to compute $P(\text{cross})$.
:::

You should find
$$p = P(\text{cross}) = \frac{2\ell}{\pi t}.$$
Now $\pi$ sits inside a probability that we can estimate by dropping needles.

### The estimator

If $C$ of $N$ needles cross a line, the fraction $\hat p = C/N$ is an average of independent indicators, exactly like the circle estimator. So $\hat p$ is unbiased for $p$, and the analysis of @exr-pi-variance applies to it. Solving $p = 2\ell/(\pi t)$ for $\pi$ and substituting $\hat p$ for $p$ gives our second estimator.

::: {#def-buffon-estimator}
## Buffon's estimator
Drop $N$ needles independently, and let $C$ be the number that cross a line. Estimate $\pi$ by
$$\hat{\pi}_N = \frac{2 \ell N}{t\, C} = \frac{2\ell}{t}\cdot\frac{1}{\hat p}.$$
:::

#### Bias

::: {#exr-buffon-zero}
## An undefined estimator
If $C = 0$, the estimator is undefined: it divides by zero. Find $P(C = 0)$ in terms of $N$.
:::

You should find that this probability shrinks geometrically in $N$, so $C = 0$ is negligible in practice. **From here on, we assume that $C \ge 1$.**

The *bias* of an estimator $\hat\pi_N$ is
$$
\text{Bias}(\hat\pi_N) = \mathbb{E}[\hat\pi_N] - \pi.
$$
The circle estimator (@def-circle-estimator) is an average, so linearity gives it bias zero. Buffon's estimator instead *divides* by a random count, and since $x \mapsto 1/x$ is not linear, in general
$$
\mathbb{E}[1/\hat p] \neq 1/\mathbb{E}[\hat p].
$$
So linearity no longer computes $\mathbb{E}[\hat\pi_N]$, and Buffon's estimator is biased.

::: {#exr-buffon-bias}
## Bias
a. Expand $1/\hat p$ to second order about $p$ and take expectations to approximate $\mathbb{E}[\hat\pi_N]$ and the bias of $\hat\pi_N$, in terms of $p$ and $N$.
b. How fast does the bias shrink with $N$?
c. The second-order term in (a) comes from the convexity of $x \mapsto 1/x$. Use its sign to decide whether, for large $N$, $\hat\pi_N$ overestimates or underestimates $\pi$. Can you interpret this directly?
:::

#### Variance

For the variance, the linear term of the expansion is enough. This is the *delta method*: for a smooth function $g$, $g(\hat p) \approx g(p) + g'(p)(\hat p - p)$, so
$$
\text{Var}(g(\hat p)) \approx g'(p)^2\, \text{Var}(\hat p).
$$

::: {#exr-buffon-variance}
## Standard error
a. Using the delta method approximate $\text{Var}(\hat\pi_N)$ and $\text{SE}(\hat\pi_N)$, in terms of $p$ and $N$.
b. How does $\text{SE}(\hat\pi_N)$ grow as $\ell \to 0$?
c. Take the longest needle, $\ell = t$. How many needles does it take to match the accuracy of $N$ random points in the circle method (@exr-pi-variance)?
:::

#### Mean squared error

Because the estimator is biased, standard error is no longer a good measure of uncertainty. The *mean squared error* is the more appropriate measure in this case:
$$
\text{MSE}(\hat\pi_N) = \mathbb{E}[(\hat\pi_N - \pi)^2].
$$
In general, the MSE equals the variance plus the squared bias:
$$
\text{MSE}(\hat\pi_N) = \text{Var}(\hat\pi_N) + \text{Bias}(\hat\pi_N)^2.
$$
For an unbiased estimator the MSE is just the variance.

::: {#exr-buffon-mse}
## Mean squared error
a. Using your approximations from @exr-buffon-bias and @exr-buffon-variance, find the ratio $\text{Bias}(\hat\pi_N)/\text{SE}(\hat\pi_N)$.
b. What happens to this ratio as $N \to \infty$? Which term dominates the MSE?
c. Evaluate the bias and the standard error for $\ell = t = 1$ and $N = 100$.
:::

You should find that even though the estimator is biased, the bias becomes negligible compared to the standard error as $N$ grows. The MSE is then essentially the variance, so dividing by a random count changes the constant but not the $O(N^{-1/2})$ rate of the error.

@fig-buffon-convergence repeats the two experiments of @fig-pi-convergence for Buffon's estimator. The plots should look like the circle estimator's: the running estimates settle on $\pi$, and the error falls along a line of slope $-1/2$ on the log-log plot. Only the constant differs, and it depends on $\ell$. Move the slider to change $\ell$ and watch the plots follow.

::: {#rem-noodle .remark}
## The shape does not matter
Bend the needle into any curve of length $\ell$. Cut it into many short straight pieces: each is a short needle placed uniformly at random, so it crosses a line with expected count $2/(\pi t)$ times its length. By linearity of expectation (which holds even though the pieces are dependent), $\mathbb{E}[\text{crossings per drop}] = 2\ell/(\pi t)$ for every shape, and $2\ell N / (t \cdot \text{total crossings})$ still estimates $\pi$. This is Barbier's 1860 observation. Switch the *Shape* in [the app](#buffon-app) to *Noodle*, a zigzag of three straight pieces, to see the estimate still converge to $\pi$. Linearity is a property of expectation alone, though: the variance, and with it the bias, does depend on the shape.
:::


## Randomness is slow

Both random methods converge at the Monte Carlo rate $O(N^{-1/2})$ (@exr-pi-variance, @exr-buffon-mse), so each extra decimal digit costs a hundred times more samples. That is far too slow to compute $\pi$ in practice: the two methods are proofs of concept, not practical algorithms. Non-random methods do much better. We start with two that still count points in the disk, and end with a table of standard numerical methods.


```{ojs}
//| output: false
gaussMaxR = 40
gaussDefaultR = 8
gaussTraceOptions = ["Inside", "Outside", "Circle"]
gaussTraceColors = new Map([
  ["Inside", chartColors.fn],
  ["Outside", chartColors.muted],
  ["Circle", chartColors.ink]
])

haltonMaxN = 10000
haltonDefaultN = 1000
haltonTraceOptions = ["Inside", "Outside", "Circle and square"]
haltonTraceColors = new Map([
  ["Inside", chartColors.fn],
  ["Outside", chartColors.warn],
  ["Circle and square", chartColors.ink]
])

// The circle x² + y² = r², for drawing only.
function circlePath(r) {
  const xs = [], ys = []
  for (let k = 0; k <= 200; k++) {
    xs.push(r * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * k / 200))
    ys.push(r * Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * k / 200))
  }
  return {xs, ys}
}
```

### The Gauss circle method

Gauss came up with a simple idea to measure the area of a circle: count the integer points $(x, y)$ with $x^2 + y^2 \le r^2$, and call the count $L(r)$. This approximates the disk's area $\pi r^2$, and
$$
\hat\pi_r = \frac{L(r)}{r^2}
$$
estimates $\pi$.

{
  const r = gaussR

Counting the points one at a time takes a double loop over the $(2r + 1)^2$ points of the grid. Can we do better?

::: {#exr-gauss-count}
## Counting is cheap
Show that
$$
L(r) = \sum_{x=-r}^{r} \left(2\left\lfloor\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}\right\rfloor + 1\right),
$$
so $\hat\pi_r = L(r)/r^2$ needs only one loop over $x$, of $2r + 1$ steps.
:::



### Halton points

Gauss's method is a grid: its points come all at once, $(2r + 1)^2$ of them, and the one-loop trick of @exr-gauss-count relies on the shape of the disk. Can we keep the grid's even coverage, but add points one at a time, as with random points?

The *Halton sequence* does this. Each new point roughly fills the gaps left by the earlier ones, so the first $N$ points cover the square evenly for every $N$. The points are not random at all: they are spread more evenly than random points would be. Such points are called *quasi-random*, and using them in place of random points is called *quasi-Monte Carlo*. The app below uses them in the circle estimator $4 \cdot (\text{inside})/N$.

### Comparing the three

@fig-pi-methods plots each method's error on log-log axes, against the number of points $N$ for random and Halton points, and against the radius $r$, the length of the loop in @exr-gauss-count, for the Gauss circle method.


```{ojs}
//| output: false
cmpMaxN = 1e5
cmpCounts = checkpoints(cmpMaxN)
cmpSeries = [
  {label: "Random points", token: "fn", points: randomCircleErrors(VM.sampling.seededRandom(7), cmpCounts, 40), scatter: false},
  {label: "Gauss circle (against r)", token: "warn", points: latticeErrors(cmpMaxN), scatter: true},
  {label: "Halton points", token: "ok", points: haltonCircleErrors(checkpoints(cmpMaxN, 24)), scatter: true}
]
```


::: {#fig-pi-methods}


```{ojs}
{
  const marks = []
  const key = []
  let lo = Infinity, hi = 0, xLo = Infinity
  for (const s of cmpSeries) {
    const color = chartColors[s.token]
    xLo = Math.min(xLo, s.points[0].n)
    key.push({label: s.label, color})
    // A deterministic error can land exactly on π, which a log axis can't show.
    const rows = []
    for (const p of s.points) {
      if (p.error > 0) rows.push(p)
    }
    for (const p of rows) {
      lo = Math.min(lo, p.error)
      hi = Math.max(hi, p.error)
    }
    if (s.scatter) {
      // The deterministic errors swing from one N to the next, so their points
      // stay unjoined and their rate is drawn as the fitted line instead:
      // solid over the fitted range N ≥ 100, dashed where it is extended back
      // to the first point.
      const fit = convergenceFit(s.points)
      const fitLine = n => 10 ** fit.intercept * n ** -fit.order
      const first = s.points[0].n
      const last = s.points[s.points.length - 1].n
      marks.push(Plot.dot(rows, {x: "n", y: "error", fill: color, r: 1.5}))
      marks.push(Plot.line([{n: 100, error: fitLine(100)}, {n: last, error: fitLine(last)}], {x: "n", y: "error", stroke: color, strokeWidth: 2}))
      marks.push(Plot.line([{n: first, error: fitLine(first)}, {n: 100, error: fitLine(100)}], {x: "n", y: "error", stroke: color, strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "6,4"}))
    } else {
      // The 10%-90% band, clamped above zero for the log axis.
      const band = []
      for (const p of s.points) band.push({n: p.n, lo: Math.max(p.lo, 1e-9), hi: p.hi})
      marks.push(Plot.areaY(band, {x: "n", y1: "lo", y2: "hi", fill: VM.plotting.alpha(color, 0.15), clip: true}))
      marks.push(Plot.line(rows, {x: "n", y: "error", stroke: color, strokeWidth: 2}))
      marks.push(Plot.dot(rows, {x: "n", y: "error", fill: color, r: 2.5}))
    }
  }
  // Reference slopes N⁻¹ᐟ² (dashed) and N⁻¹ (dotted), labelled at their right end.
  const references = [
    {label: "N⁻¹ᐟ²", dash: "6,4", points: [{n: 10, error: 1}, {n: cmpMaxN, error: Math.sqrt(10 / cmpMaxN)}]},
    {label: "N⁻¹", dash: "2,3", points: [{n: 10, error: 0.3}, {n: cmpMaxN, error: 0.3 * 10 / cmpMaxN}]}
  ]
  for (const ref of references) {
    marks.push(Plot.line(ref.points, {x: "n", y: "error", stroke: chartColors.muted, strokeWidth: 1, strokeDasharray: ref.dash}))
    marks.push(Plot.text([ref.points[1]], {x: "n", y: "error", text: () => ref.label, textAnchor: "start", dx: 4, fill: chartColors.muted}))
    lo = Math.min(lo, ref.points[1].error)
    hi = Math.max(hi, ref.points[0].error)
  }
  const chart = Plot.plot(VM.plotting.plotOptions({
    width, height: 420, marginLeft: 50, marginRight: 40, marginBottom: 40,
    x: piLogAxis(xLo, cmpMaxN, {label: "N (points), or r for Gauss", labelAnchor: "center", tickFormat: "~s"}),
    y: piLogAxis(lo, hi, {label: "|estimate − π|"}, 1.25),
    marks
  }))
  return piFigure(chart, key)
}
```

### Other numerical methods for $\pi$

The table compares the methods on this page with deterministic ones, from slowest to fastest.

| Method | π is | Error | App |
|---|---|---|---|
| Circle method (random points) | 4 × P(a uniform point of the square lands in the disk) | $O(N^{-1/2})$ | [above](#pi-app) |
| Buffon's needle / Barbier's noodle | 2ℓ / (t × mean crossings per drop) | $O(N^{-1/2})$ | [above](#buffon-app) |
| Circle method (Halton points) | 4 × fraction of Halton points in the disk | about $O(N^{-3/4})$ | [above](#halton-app) |
| Gauss circle method | lattice points in the disk of radius r, divided by r² | $O(r^{-1})$ proven, about $O(r^{-3/2})$ conjectured | [above](#gauss-app) |
| Linear interpolation | the length of y = √(1 − x²) over [−1, 1], a semicircle | $O(N^{-3/2})$ | [Linear interpolation of the semicircle](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/polynomial-interpolation/index.html?embed=1&f=sqrt(1-x%5E2)&a=-1&b=1&max=40&n=8&show=original,linear,nodes){target="_blank"} |
| Cubic spline | the length of y = √(1 − x²) over [−1, 1] | $O(N^{-3/2})$ | [Cubic spline of the semicircle](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/polynomial-interpolation/index.html?embed=1&f=sqrt(1-x%5E2)&a=-1&b=1&max=40&n=8&show=original,cubic,nodes){target="_blank"} |
| Adaptive Simpson | ∫₀¹ 4/(1 + x²) dx | $O(N^{-6})$ | [Adaptive integration of 4/(1 + x²)](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/adaptive-integration/index.html?embed=1&f=4%2F(1%2Bx%5E2)&a=0&b=1){target="_blank"} |
| Adaptive Simpson | ∫₀¹ 4√(1 − x²) dx, four quarter disks | $O(N^{-6})$ | [Adaptive integration of 4√(1 − x²)](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/adaptive-integration/index.html?embed=1&f=4*sqrt(1-x%5E2)&a=0&b=1){target="_blank"} |
| Adaptive Simpson | (∫₋₆⁶ e^−x²^ dx)² | $O(N^{-6})$ | [Adaptive integration of e^−x²^](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/adaptive-integration/index.html?embed=1&f=exp(-x%5E2)&a=-6&b=6){target="_blank"} |
| Trapezoid rule | (∫₋₆⁶ e^−x²^ dx)² | $O(e^{-cN^2})$ | [Trapezoid on e^−x²^](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/numerical-integration/index.html?embed=1&f=exp(-x%5E2)&a=-6&b=6&max=40&n=12&show=f,trapezoidal){target="_blank"} |
| Newton's method | the root of sin x, starting from 1.98 | $O(e^{-c\,3^{N/2}})$ | [Newton on sin x](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/newton-method/index.html?embed=1&f=sin(x)&x0=1.98&max=12){target="_blank"} |
| Fixed-point iteration | the fixed point of x + sin x, starting from 0.1 | $O(e^{-c\,3^N})$ | [Iterating x + sin x](https://www.visualmathlab.com/apps/fixed-point-iteration/index.html?embed=1&g=x%2Bsin(x)&x0=0.1&max=12){target="_blank"} |


## Summary

- **The Monte Carlo principle.** Write a deterministic quantity as the expectation of a random variable, then estimate it by a sample average.
- **The Monte Carlo rate.** An average of $N$ i.i.d. samples with finite variance is unbiased, with standard error proportional to $N^{-1/2}$. Each extra digit costs a hundred times more samples, whatever the problem.

The next chapter, [Estimating integrals](../integrals/), applies the same principle to integrals, where the dimension of the problem decides whether randomness pays off.
